{{Short description|Complex vector of electromagnetic fields}}
{{electromagnetism}}

In [[mathematical physics]], in particular [[electromagnetism]], the '''Riemann–Silberstein vector'''<ref name=bial /> or '''Weber vector'''<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Michael K.-H. Kiessling and A. Shadi Tahvildar-Zadeh|year=2018 |title=On the quantum-mechanics of a single photon|arxiv=1801.00268|journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |volume=59 |issue=11 |pages=112302|doi=10.1063/1.5021066|bibcode=2018JMP....59k2302K |s2cid=51030338 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |author=Charles T. Sebens|year=2019 |title=Electromagnetism as Quantum Physics|arxiv=1902.01930 |journal=Foundations of Physics |volume=49 |issue= 4|pages=365–389|doi=10.1007/s10701-019-00253-3|bibcode=2019FoPh...49..365S |s2cid=84846425 }}</ref> named after [[Bernhard Riemann]], [[Heinrich Martin Weber]] and [[Ludwik Silberstein]], (or sometimes ambiguously called the "electromagnetic field") is a [[complex number|complex]] [[vector space|vector]] that combines the [[electric field]] '''E''' and the [[magnetic field]] '''B'''.

==History==
[[Heinrich Martin Weber]] published the fourth edition of "The [[partial differential equations]] of mathematical physics according to Riemann's lectures" in two volumes (1900 and 1901). However, Weber pointed out in the preface of the first volume (1900) that this fourth edition was completely rewritten based on his own lectures, not Riemann's, and that the reference to "Riemann's lectures" only remained in the title because the overall concept remained the same and that he continued the work in Riemann's spirit.<ref>{{Cite book |author=Weber, Heinrich Martin|year=1900|title=Die partiellen Differential-Gleichungen der mathematischen Physik nach Riemann's Vorlesungen (4. edition, volume I)|location=Braunschweig|publisher=Vieweg|url=https://archive.org/details/diepartiellendi03webegoog}}</ref> In the second volume (1901, §138, p.&nbsp;348), Weber demonstrated how to consolidate Maxwell's equations using <math>\mathfrak{E} + i\ \mathfrak{M}</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |author=Weber, Heinrich Martin|year=1901|title=Die partiellen Differential-Gleichungen der mathematischen Physik nach Riemann's Vorlesungen (4. edition, volume II)|location=Braunschweig|publisher=Vieweg|url=https://archive.org/details/diepartiellendi01riemgoog}}</ref> The real and imaginary components of the equation
:<math>\operatorname{curl}(\mathfrak{E} + i\ \mathfrak{M}) = \frac{i}{c}\ \frac {\partial (\mathfrak{E} + i\ \mathfrak{M})} {\partial t} </math>
are an interpretation of Maxwell's equations without charges or currents. It was independently rediscovered and further developed by [[Ludwik Silberstein]] in 1907.<ref>

==Definition==
Given an electric field '''E''' and a magnetic field '''B''' defined on a common [[region (mathematical analysis)|region]] of [[spacetime]], the Riemann–Silberstein vector is
<math display="block">\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{E} + ic \mathbf{B} ,</math>
where {{math|''c''}} is the [[speed of light]], with some authors preferring to multiply the right hand side by an overall constant <math display="inline"> \sqrt{\varepsilon_0 / 2}</math>, where {{math|''ε''<sub>0</sub>}} is the [[permittivity of free space]].  It is analogous to the [[electromagnetic tensor]] ''F'', a [[2-vector]] used in the [[covariant formulation of classical electromagnetism]].

In Silberstein's formulation, ''i'' was defined as the [[imaginary unit]], and '''F''' was defined as a [[complexified]] 3-dimensional [[vector field]], called a ''[[bivector (complex)|bivector]] field''.<ref>
{{cite journal
 |last=Aste |first=Andreas
 |year=2012
 |title=Complex representation theory of the electromagnetic field
 |journal=[[Journal of Geometry and Symmetry in Physics]]
 |volume=28 |pages=47–58
 |doi=10.7546/jgsp-28-2012-47-58
|arxiv = 1211.1218 |s2cid=119575012
 }}</ref>

==Application==

{{main article|Maxwell's equations}}
The Riemann–Silberstein vector is used as a point of reference in the [[mathematical descriptions of the electromagnetic field#Geometric algebra formulations|geometric algebra formulation of electromagnetism]].  Maxwell's ''four'' equations in [[vector calculus]] reduce to ''one'' equation in the [[algebra of physical space]]:

:<math> \left(\frac{1}{c}\dfrac{\partial }{\partial t} + \boldsymbol{\nabla}\right)\mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{\epsilon_0}\left( \rho - \frac{1}{c}\mathbf{J} \right).</math>

Expressions for the [[classification of electromagnetic fields#Invariants|fundamental invariants]] and the [[energy density#Energy density of electric and magnetic fields|energy density]] and [[momentum]] density also take on simple forms:

:<math> \mathbf{F}^2 = \mathbf{E}^2 - c^2\mathbf{B}^2 + 2 i c\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{B}</math>
:<math> \frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\mathbf{F}^{\dagger}  \mathbf{F} = \frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\left( \mathbf{E}^2 + c^2\mathbf{B}^2 \right) + \frac{1}{c} \mathbf{S},</math>

where '''S''' is the [[Poynting vector]]. See also [[Spacetime algebra]] for further examples of the above product notation. 

The Riemann–Silberstein vector is used for an [[Matrix Representation of Maxwell Equations|exact matrix representations of Maxwell's equations in an inhomogeneous medium with sources]].<ref name=bial>

==Photon wave function==
In 1996 contribution<ref name=bial/> to [[quantum electrodynamics]], Iwo Bialynicki-Birula used the Riemann–Silberstein vector as the basis for an approach to the [[photon]], noting that it is a "complex vector-function of space coordinates '''r''' and time ''t'' that adequately describes the [[quantum state]] of a single photon". To put the Riemann–Silberstein vector in contemporary parlance, a transition is made:
:With the advent of [[spinor]] calculus that superseded the quaternionic  calculus, the transformation properties of the Riemann-Silberstein vector have become even more transparent ... a symmetric second-rank spinor.
Bialynicki-Birula acknowledges that the photon wave function is a controversial concept and that it cannot have all the properties of [[Schrödinger equation|Schrödinger]] [[wave function]]s of non-relativistic wave mechanics. Yet defense is mounted on the basis of practicality: it is useful for describing quantum states of excitation of a free field, electromagnetic fields acting on a medium, vacuum excitation of virtual positron-electron pairs, and presenting the photon among quantum particles that do have wave functions.

===Schrödinger equation for the photon and the Heisenberg uncertainty relations===

Multiplying the two time dependent Maxwell equations by <math>\hbar</math> 
the  Schrödinger equation for photon in the vacuum is given by

:<math>i \hbar \partial_{t} {\mathbf F}=c (\mathbf S \cdot {\hbar \over i} \nabla) \mathbf F = c (\mathbf S \cdot \mathbf p ) \mathbf F</math>

where <math>{\mathbf S}</math> is the vector built from the [[Spin (physics)|spin]] of the length 1 [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrices]]  generating full infinitesimal rotations of 3-spinor particle. One may therefore notice that the 
Hamiltonian in the Schrödinger equation of the photon is the projection of its spin 1 onto 
its momentum since the normal momentum operator appears there from combining parts of rotations.

In contrast to the electron wave function the modulus square of the wave function of the photon 
(Riemann-Silbertein vector) is not dimensionless and must be multiplied by the "local photon
wavelength" with the proper power to give dimensionless expression to normalize i.e. 
it is normalized in the exotic way with the integral kernel
:<math>\|\mathbf F\|={1 \over \hbar c}\int {\mathbf F^*(x) \cdot \mathbf F(x') \over |x-x'|^2}dx^3 dx'^3=1</math>

The two residual Maxwell equations are only constraints i.e. 
:<math>\nabla \cdot \mathbf F=0</math>

and they are automatically fulfilled all time if only fulfilled at the initial time 
<math>t=0</math>, i.e.
:<math>\mathbf F(0)= \nabla \times \mathbf  G</math>

where <math>\mathbf G</math>
is any complex  [[vector field]] with the non-vanishing  [[Curl (mathematics)|rotation]], or 
it is a vector potential for the Riemann–Silberstein vector.

While having the wave function of the photon one can estimate the uncertainty relations 
for the photon.<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://www.cft.edu.pl/~birula/publ/PhotUncert.pdf|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.108.140401|title=Uncertainty Relation for Photon|author=Bialynicki-Birula, Iwo|journal=Phys. Rev. Lett.|volume=108|pages=140401–1–5|issue=14|year = 2012|pmid=22540772|arxiv = 1110.2415 |bibcode = 2012PhRvL.108n0401B |s2cid=30928536}}- This publication is using slightly different definitions of position and momentum uncertainties resigning from the position operator and normalizing uncertainty of <math>r^2</math> to uncertainty of r</ref> It shows up that photons are "more quantum" than the electron while their 
uncertainties of position and the momentum are higher. The natural candidates to estimate the uncertainty are the natural momentum like  simply the projection <math>E/c</math> or  <math>H/c</math> from Einstein
formula for the photoelectric effect and the simplest theory of quanta and the <math>r</math>, the uncertainty 
of the position length vector.

We will use the general relation for the uncertainty for the operators <math>A, B</math>
: <math>\sigma_{A}\sigma_{B} \geq  \frac{1}{2}\left|\langle[\hat{A},\hat{B}]\rangle \right|.</math>
We want the uncertainty relation for <math>\sigma_{r}\sigma_{p}</math> i.e. for the operators
: <math>r^2=x^2+y^2+z^2</math>
: <math>p^2=(\mathbf S \cdot \mathbf p )^2</math>

The first step is to find the auxiliary operator <math>\tilde r</math> such that this relation
can be used directly. First we  make  the same trick for <math>r</math> that Dirac made to calculate the 
square root of the Klein-Gordon operator to get the [[w:Dirac equation|Dirac equation]]:
: <math>\tilde r = \alpha_1 x + \alpha_2 y + \alpha_3 z </math>
where <math>\alpha_i</math> are [[Gamma matrices|matrices from the Dirac equation]]:
: <math>\alpha_i^2=1</math>
: <math>\alpha_i \alpha_k + \alpha_k \alpha_i= 2  \delta_{ik} </math>
Therefore, we have 
: <math>\tilde r^2 = r^2</math>
Because the spin matrices 1 are  only <math>3 \times 3</math> to calculate the commutator 
in the same space we approximate the spin matrices
by [[angular momentum]] matrices of the particle with the length <math>3/2 \approx 1</math> while 
dropping the multiplying <math>1/2</math> since the resulting Maxwell equations in 4 dimensions would look too artificial
to the original (alternatively we can keep the original <math>1/2</math> factors but normalize the new 4-spinor 
to 2 as 4 scalar particles normalized to 1/2):{{Clarification needed|reason=The justification for these approximations is unclear.|date=September 2023}}
: <math>\tilde p^2 = (\mathbf \tilde L \cdot \mathbf p)^2</math>
We can now readily calculate the commutator while calculating commutators 
of <math>\alpha_i</math> matrixes and scaled <math>\tilde L_i</math> and noticing that the symmetric [[Gaussian state]] 
<math>e^{-a r^2}</math> is annihilating in average the terms containing mixed variable like
<math>x p_y</math>.
Calculating 9 commutators (mixed may be zero by Gaussian example and the <math>L_z \alpha_z=\alpha_z L_z=0</math> since those matrices are counter-diagonal) and estimating 
terms from the norm of the resulting <math>4 \times 4</math> matrix containing four <math>2\sqrt 3</math>  factors giving square of the most natural [[matrix norm|<math>L2, 1</math> norm of this matrix]] as <math>48 \approx 49=7^2 \approx 8^2</math> {{Clarification needed|reason=What are we saying by asserting that 48 ≈ 49 = 7^2 ≈ 8^2? Why is this relevant?|date=September 2023}} and using the norm inequality  for the estimate 
:<math>\lVert\mathbf A \mathbf x\rVert \leq \lVert\mathbf A\rVert \lVert\mathbf x\rVert \approx \lVert\mathbf A\rVert \lVert\mathbf x\rVert</math>
we obtain 
:<math>\left|\langle[\tilde r,\tilde p]\rangle \right|\geq 8 \hbar .</math>
or  
:<math>\sigma_{r}\sigma_{p}\geq 4 \hbar</math>
which is much more than for the mass particle in 3 dimensions that is 
:<math>\sigma_{r}\sigma_{p}\geq \frac{3}{2}\hbar</math>
and therefore photons turn out to be particles 
<math>8/3</math> times  or almost 3 times "more quantum" than particles with the mass like electrons.{{Clarification needed|reason=What is "more quantum" supposed to mean?|date=September 2023}}
